title: Does the Mutation Stay or Travel?

scenes.tts: The first film showed a repressor moving on and off its operator. A broken repressor and broken operator can both look constitutive, so how can another lac copy tell them apart?
scenes.caption: The first film showed a repressor moving on and off its operator. A broken repressor and broken operator can both look constitutive, so how can another lac copy tell them apart?
scenes.visual: Hook picture inside the same schematic cell and colour map as the first film: red repressor, orange operator, green lac genes, yellow inducer. Place two grey DNA rails side by side. One shows a cracked red repressor icon; the other shows a cracked orange operator. Both green reporter lamps glow without inducer under one large question mark.
scenes.narration: The first film showed a repressor moving on and off its operator. A broken repressor and broken operator can both look constitutive, so how can another lac copy tell them apart?

scenes.visual: Keep both DNA rails drifting gently. Add the title ‘Does the Mutation Stay or Travel?’ for two seconds, then dissolve it while preserving the rails. Label the diagram ‘schematic’.

scenes.tts: Geneticists place a chromosomal lac region and an F prime lac copy in one cell. This partial diploid is diploid only for that region. Each rail carries its own operator and lac Z reporter. Both DNA copies share the same pool of regulatory proteins.
scenes.caption: Geneticists place a chromosomal lac region and an F′ lac copy in one cell. This partial diploid is diploid only for that region. Each rail carries its own operator and lacZ reporter. Both DNA copies share the same pool of regulatory proteins.
scenes.visual: Transform the left rail into a long chromosome loop and the right rail into a smaller F′ loop. Zoom their lac regions into parallel rails. Each has an orange operator block and a green lacZ reporter ending in a large lamp. Keep the objects large and centred.
scenes.narration: Geneticists place a chromosomal lac region and an F′ lac copy in one cell. This partial diploid is diploid only for that region. Each rail carries its own operator and lacZ reporter. Both DNA copies share the same pool of regulatory proteins.

scenes.tts: Read the reporter before judging the mutation. Find the working lac Z. Then check the operator beside it. Finally ask which repressor proteins anywhere in the cell can reach that operator. This order prevents a broken reporter from misleading you.
scenes.caption: Read the reporter before judging the mutation. Find the working lacZ. Then check the operator beside it. Finally ask which repressor proteins anywhere in the cell can reach that operator. This order prevents a broken reporter from misleading you.
scenes.visual: A bright focus ring moves in sequence: first around a green Z+ reporter, then its adjacent orange operator, then around several red repressors moving through the shared cell. A compact vertical checklist grows beside the rails: ‘reporter’, ‘linked operator’, ‘reachable repressor’.
scenes.narration: Read the reporter before judging the mutation. Find the working lacZ. Then check the operator beside it. Finally ask which repressor proteins anywhere in the cell can reach that operator. This order prevents a broken reporter from misleading you.

scenes.tts: Start with a lac I minus allele that makes no working repressor. A normal lac I on the other rail makes red repressor protein. That protein diffuses through the shared cell and binds either normal operator. The missing product arrives from the other copy, so the defect is complemented. Lac I minus is recessive. Inducer can still release the repressor.
scenes.caption: Start with a lacI− allele that makes no working repressor. A normal lacI on the other rail makes red repressor protein. That protein diffuses through the shared cell and binds either normal operator. The missing product arrives from the other copy, so the defect is complemented. lacI− is recessive. Inducer can still release the repressor.
scenes.visual: On the chromosome, show lacI− as a crossed red repressor factory, without saying the whole DNA is rejected. On F′, a normal lacI factory releases red repressor cartoons. They travel along curved paths to both orange normal operators. Yellow inducer badges open the clamps on both rails.
scenes.narration: Start with a lacI− allele that makes no working repressor. A normal lacI on the other rail makes red repressor protein. That protein diffuses through the shared cell and binds either normal operator. The missing product arrives from the other copy, so the defect is complemented. lacI− is recessive. Inducer can still release the repressor.

scenes.tts: Now change an operator itself. The altered orange block never leaves its rail. No other copy can supply a working site. The site cannot diffuse, so its effect stays beside linked genes. A linked working reporter escapes repression. A reporter beside the normal operator remains inducible.
scenes.caption: Now change an operator itself. The altered orange block never leaves its rail. No other copy can supply a working site. The site cannot diffuse, so its effect stays beside linked genes. A linked working reporter escapes repression. A reporter beside the normal operator remains inducible.
scenes.visual: Crack the orange operator on the chromosome while red repressors continue roaming. They fail to grip only that orange block. Its adjacent green Z+ lamp glows continuously. The F′ operator remains intact; a red clamp binds there and its adjacent lamp responds to yellow inducer.
scenes.narration: Now change an operator itself. The altered orange block never leaves its rail. No other copy can supply a working site. The site cannot diffuse, so its effect stays beside linked genes. A linked working reporter escapes repression. A reporter beside the normal operator remains inducible.

scenes.tts: Predict this arrangement. The only working reporter sits beside a normal operator. Normal repressor comes from the other DNA rail. Will the reporter remain controllable by inducer?
scenes.caption: Predict this arrangement. The only working reporter sits beside a normal operator. Normal repressor comes from the other DNA rail. Will the reporter remain controllable by inducer?
scenes.visual: Reset both lamps to neutral. Put Z+ beside a normal orange operator on F′ and Z− beside an altered operator on the chromosome. A normal lacI factory on the chromosome releases one red repressor. Hold a large question above the F′ lamp.
scenes.narration: Predict this arrangement. The only working reporter sits beside a normal operator. Normal repressor comes from the other DNA rail. Will the reporter remain controllable by inducer?

scenes.visual: Keep the question visible. Let the red repressor drift slowly between rails without reaching an operator yet. Do not reveal either reporter state.

scenes.tts: Yes. The normal repressor reaches the normal operator beside the working reporter. Without inducer, it holds transcription at a low basal level. With inducer, the clamp opens and the reporter turns on. The cell is inducible for active enzyme. The altered operator is linked only to a broken reporter.
scenes.caption: Yes. The normal repressor reaches the normal operator beside the working reporter. Without inducer, it holds transcription at a low basal level. With inducer, the clamp opens and the reporter turns on. The cell is inducible for active enzyme. The altered operator is linked only to a broken reporter.
scenes.visual: Animate the red clamp onto the F′ normal operator and hold its green Z+ lamp at a faint basal glow, not fully dark. A yellow inducer badge opens the clamp; polymerase passes and the lamp glows. Keep the chromosome’s altered operator beside Z−, whose lamp stays dark because the reporter is broken.
scenes.narration: Yes. The normal repressor reaches the normal operator beside the working reporter. Without inducer, it holds transcription at a low basal level. With inducer, the clamp opens and the reporter turns on. The cell is inducible for active enzyme. The altered operator is linked only to a broken reporter.

scenes.tts: Swap the reporters while leaving both operators fixed. Now the working reporter sits beside the altered operator. It glows with or without inducer. The phenotype follows the reporter's linkage to the DNA site, not a signal travelling across the cell.
scenes.caption: Swap the reporters while leaving both operators fixed. Now the working reporter sits beside the altered operator. It glows with or without inducer. The phenotype follows the reporter's linkage to the DNA site, not a signal travelling across the cell.
scenes.visual: Slide the green Z+ and grey Z− blocks across the parallel rails while both orange operators stay anchored. Once Z+ locks beside the altered operator, its lamp rises to steady green under both ‘inducer absent’ and ‘inducer present’ labels. Trace a short gold bracket joining that operator to its reporter.
scenes.narration: Swap the reporters while leaving both operators fixed. Now the working reporter sits beside the altered operator. It glows with or without inducer. The phenotype follows the reporter's linkage to the DNA site, not a signal travelling across the cell.

scenes.tts: Notice what this test never needed: a purified repressor. Geneticists mapped a travelling product before anyone knew what it was made of. Biochemists later isolated it and found a protein. The genetic rules did not change.
scenes.caption: Notice what this test never needed: a purified repressor. Geneticists mapped a travelling product before anyone knew what it was made of. Biochemists later isolated it and found a protein. The genetic rules did not change.
scenes.visual: Keep the two rails and the roaming red repressors. Freeze one red repressor and wrap it in a dashed outline labelled ‘inferred from genetics’. Then fill the outline in solid red and add a small label ‘isolated later: a protein’. The rails and arrows stay unchanged. Label the diagram ‘schematic’.
scenes.narration: Notice what this test never needed: a purified repressor. Geneticists mapped a travelling product before anyone knew what it was made of. Biochemists later isolated it and found a protein. The genetic rules did not change.

scenes.tts: Partial diploids turn location into evidence. An effect limited to its own DNA copy is called cis, pointing to a local control site. An effect carried across both copies by a diffusing product is trans, pointing to a regulator. Always read the working reporter first.
scenes.caption: Partial diploids turn location into evidence. An effect limited to its own DNA copy is called cis, pointing to a local control site. An effect carried across both copies by a diffusing product is trans, pointing to a regulator. Always read the working reporter first.
scenes.visual: Transform the rails into a final comparison. Left: an orange operator anchored to one rail with a short bracket labelled ‘cis’. Right: red repressors moving between rails with arrows labelled ‘trans’. The checklist highlights ‘working reporter first’. Add on-screen definitions as each term is spoken: 'cis = same copy only' on the left and 'trans = across copies' on the right.
scenes.narration: Partial diploids turn location into evidence. An effect limited to its own DNA copy is called cis, pointing to a local control site. An effect carried across both copies by a diffusing product is trans, pointing to a regulator. Always read the working reporter first.

scenes.visual: One-line end card only, centred large on the dark background: 'DNA sites act in cis; diffusible regulators can act in trans.'
